name: Tesofensine
used_for: A small-molecule serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine reuptake inhibitor, not a peptide. It was first studied for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, where weight loss emerged as an effect, and was then studied for obesity, including a combination with metoprolol (Tesomet). A phase 2 trial found weight loss beyond diet alone, with dry mouth, insomnia and heart rate increases reported. Wikipedia states it has no approval for sale anywhere.

entries.text: In a 2008 phase 2 trial, tesofensine 0.25 mg, 0.5 mg or 1.0 mg was given once daily for 24 weeks with an energy-restricted diet.
In a 2022 trial, Tesomet (tesofensine 0.5 mg with metoprolol 50 mg) was given for 24 weeks with diet and lifestyle counselling.
In a 2010 randomized study, tesofensine 2.0 mg daily was given for 7 days, then 1.0 mg daily for 7 days.

internet_entries.text: A peptide site with affiliate links and vendor discount codes says community protocols cluster at 0.5 mg per day, with 0.25 mg per day for the first one to two weeks to check tolerance.
internet_entries.population: As described by the source, not a study population

administration_guidance.text: A Wikipedia summary lists dry mouth, headache, nausea, insomnia, diarrhea and constipation as common adverse events with tesofensine, and notes small blood pressure and heart rate increases.
administration_guidance.label: internet

side_effects.text: In a 24-week phase 2 trial in 203 obese adults, the most common adverse events with tesofensine were dry mouth, nausea, constipation, hard stools, diarrhea and insomnia, and heart rate rose by 7.4 beats per minute in one dose group.
side_effects.label: research

side_effects.text: In a small randomized trial of Tesomet (tesofensine with metoprolol) in hypothalamic obesity, related events were mostly mild: sleep disturbances (50% vs 13% placebo), dry mouth (43% vs 0%) and headache (36% vs 0%), with one serious event of worsened anxiety.
side_effects.label: research

internet_claims.claim: Wikipedia says tesofensine originated at NeuroSearch, was redirected to obesity after weight loss was reported in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's trials, and has not been approved for sale anywhere.
Wikipedia reports phase 2b trial weight losses roughly double those of approved drugs available in 2008, with small blood pressure changes and heart rate increases of up to about 8 beats per minute.

research.summary: Phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT00394667) of tesofensine for 24 weeks with an energy-restricted diet in 203 obese adults at Danish centers.
research.finding: Weight loss was greater than diet and placebo (about 2%) in all tesofensine groups, up to about 10.6% in the highest dose group; adverse events included dry mouth, nausea, constipation, insomnia and a heart rate increase.

research.summary: Randomized placebo-controlled trial of Tesomet (tesofensine with metoprolol) for 24 weeks in 21 adults with hypothalamic obesity.
research.finding: Tesomet produced about 6.3% additional weight loss vs placebo with no significant heart rate or blood pressure differences; the trial was very small.

research.summary: Randomized placebo-controlled study of tesofensine's effect on energy metabolism and appetite in overweight and obese adults.
research.finding: In 32 overweight men over 2 weeks, tesofensine produced about 1.8 kg more weight loss than placebo and higher satiety ratings; the abstract excerpt reviewed did not show a significant effect on total 24-hour energy expenditure. Small, short study.

research.summary: Registry record for the phase 2 trial of tesofensine on weight reduction in obese patients (completed).
research.finding: Confirms the trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.

research.summary: Meta-analysis of four randomized, double-blind trials (740 on tesofensine, 228 on placebo) in Parkinson's or Alzheimer's disease, oral once daily for 14 weeks without a weight-loss program. Astrup et al., Obesity.
research.finding: Weight change after 14 weeks was +0.5% on placebo and -0.5, -0.9, -1.8 and -2.8% at 0.125, 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0 mg; heart rate rose 2.1 to 6.8 beats per minute versus placebo from 0.25 mg up, with no blood pressure effect.

research.summary: Population pharmacokinetic model from a 14-week study with multiple oral dosing in 320 patients with Alzheimer's disease. Lehr et al., Br J Clin Pharmacol.
research.finding: Modelled half-lives were 234 hours for tesofensine and 374 hours for its main metabolite M1; sex and kidney function changed steady-state exposure (women with reduced kidney function had 62% higher exposure).

research.summary: PET imaging study of dopamine transporter occupancy after oral multiple doses of 0.125 to 1 mg tesofensine for 8 to 12 days. Appel et al., Eur Neuropsychopharmacol.
research.finding: Striatal dopamine transporter occupancy rose with dose from 18% to 77%, with a maximum near 80%; the authors suggest weight loss was partly mediated by dopamine pathway changes.

research.summary: Mouse and rat experiments using behavior, electrophysiology, optogenetics and chemogenetics. Perez et al., PLoS One.
research.finding: Tesofensine inhibited a subset of GABAergic neurons in the lateral hypothalamus that promote feeding, and prolonged 5-HTP-induced weight loss and blocked the weight rebound that often follows weight loss in rats.

research.summary: Single-dose randomized, double-blind crossover study in 52 recreational stimulant users comparing tesofensine with placebo, d-amphetamine, bupropion and atomoxetine. Schoedel et al., Clin Pharmacol Ther.
research.finding: Tesofensine effects were not significantly different from placebo and the authors concluded abuse potential is no greater than bupropion or atomoxetine; single dose only.

research.summary: Lancet notice titled 'Expression of concern' for the 2008 phase 2 tesofensine obesity trial. A reply by the trial authors titled 'Under-reporting of adverse effects of tesofensine' (PMID 23849924) followed in July 2013.
research.finding: The journal flagged the 2008 trial publication with an expression of concern. The notice text itself was not available to review here, so the reasons are not stated.

research.summary: Registry record for a 21-person phase 2 trial of tesofensine 0.5 mg with metoprolol 50 mg in hypothalamic injury-induced obesity: 24 weeks double-blind, then an optional 24-week open-label extension (48 weeks total).
research.finding: Shows the longest planned human exposure found (48 weeks), with the second half uncontrolled.

dose.summary: Not approved. Trials gave tesofensine 0.25 to 1.0 mg by mouth once daily in adults with obesity. Online sources describe 0.5 mg a day as the usual level, which matches the doses studied.

items.text: Phase 2 trial: 0.25, 0.5 or 1.0 mg once daily for 24 weeks with a restricted diet in 203 adults with obesity. Weight loss beyond diet and placebo was 4.5%, 9.2% and 10.6%.
items.label: research

items.text: Meta-analysis of four 14-week trials in Parkinson's or Alzheimer's disease tested 0.125, 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0 mg once daily.
items.label: research

items.text: Tesomet (tesofensine 0.5 mg with metoprolol 50 mg) was given for 24 weeks with diet and lifestyle counselling in 21 adults with hypothalamic obesity.
items.label: research

items.text: In a 2010 randomized study, tesofensine 2.0 mg daily was given for 7 days, then 1.0 mg daily for 7 days, in 32 overweight or obese men.
items.label: research

items.text: A peptide site with affiliate links and vendor discount codes says community protocols cluster at 0.5 mg per day, with 0.25 mg per day for the first one to two weeks to check tolerance.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with affiliate links to sellers, says 0.25 mg and 0.5 mg once daily were the main doses in phase 2 and phase 3, and that 1.0 mg showed higher blood pressure and dropout rates.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide List, a site that links to prescribing providers, says 0.5 mg shows the best balance of effect and side effects, with trials using 0.25 to 1.0 mg daily.
items.label: internet

timing.summary: Trials gave one oral dose a day, and the abstracts reviewed do not state the time of day. Online sources suggest mornings to avoid trouble sleeping, which has not been tested.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with affiliate links to sellers, says trial protocols generally used morning dosing, because tesofensine raises noradrenaline and dopamine, which can disrupt sleep if taken later.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide List, a site that links to prescribing providers, says it is taken once daily, typically in the morning, to limit sleep disruption.
items.label: internet

frequency.summary: Trials used one dose once a day. Tesofensine stays in the body very long (modelled half-life about 10 days), so levels build slowly and a missed dose matters little, according to an online source.

items.text: Once-daily oral dosing was used for 24 weeks in the phase 2 obesity trial.
items.label: research

items.text: In 320 patients with Alzheimer's disease, modelled half-lives were 234 hours for tesofensine and 374 hours for its main metabolite, so steady levels take weeks to build.
items.label: research

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with affiliate links to sellers, says a single missed dose has almost no effect on blood levels at steady state, and that trial guidance was to take the next scheduled dose without doubling up. It also says levels build up over the first 4 to 6 weeks.
items.label: internet

cycle_length.summary: The longest controlled trials ran 24 weeks. A 48-week study with an uncontrolled second half was registered. No data were found on what happens after stopping.

items.text: The phase 2 obesity trial ran 24 weeks; 79% of participants completed it.
items.label: research

items.text: Four trials in Parkinson's or Alzheimer's disease lasted 14 weeks.
items.label: research

items.text: A registered 21-person trial of tesofensine with metoprolol planned 24 weeks double-blind plus a 24-week open-label extension, 48 weeks in total.
items.label: research

items.text: In rats, tesofensine blocked the weight rebound that often follows weight loss. This is animal data only.
items.label: research

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with affiliate links to sellers, says phase 2 and the Mexican phase 3 study used 24-week treatment periods and that data beyond 24 weeks are limited.
items.label: internet

storage_and_handling.summary: No study or regulator document was found on storage. Online sources describe room-temperature storage of tablets or capsules, away from light and moisture.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with affiliate links to sellers, says tablets are typically stable at room temperature (15 to 25 C) in a closed container away from light, moisture and heat, with no reconstitution needed.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide List, a site that links to prescribing providers, says to store it in a cool, dry place away from light and moisture, in its original container.
items.label: internet

mechanism.summary: Blocks the reuptake of three brain chemicals (serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine), which lowers appetite. In people, brain scans show it occupies the dopamine transporter in a dose-dependent way.

items.text: PET scans after 8 to 12 days of oral dosing showed dopamine transporter occupancy of 18% to 77% across 0.125 to 1 mg, with a ceiling near 80%.
items.label: research

items.text: In 32 overweight men, 2 weeks of tesofensine raised fullness ratings, lowered expected food intake and raised overnight energy expenditure by 4.6%, with no significant change in total 24-hour energy expenditure.
items.label: research

items.text: In mice and rats, tesofensine inhibited feeding-promoting GABAergic neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. This is animal evidence.
items.label: research

items.text: Wikipedia says tesofensine is a serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine reuptake inhibitor that mainly acts as an appetite suppressant. It says it originated at NeuroSearch and was redirected to obesity after weight loss was reported in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's trials.
items.label: internet

best_documented_effect.summary: Greater weight loss than diet and placebo in a phase 2 trial of 203 adults. The main trial paper carries a journal expression of concern, and no phase 3 results were found.

items.text: In 203 adults with obesity over 24 weeks, 0.5 mg gave 9.2% weight loss and 1.0 mg gave 10.6%, versus 2.0% with diet and placebo.
items.label: research

items.text: Across four 14-week trials without any diet program, tesofensine 0.5 mg changed weight by -1.8% versus +0.5% on placebo, a difference of about 2.3 points.
items.label: research

items.text: Tesomet gave about 6.3% additional weight loss versus placebo over 24 weeks in 21 adults with hypothalamic obesity. The trial was very small.
items.label: research

items.text: The journal that published the 2008 obesity trial issued an expression of concern about it in 2013. The reasons were not available to review here.
items.label: research

items.text: Wikipedia reports phase 2b weight losses roughly double those of approved drugs available in 2008.

side_effect_groups.title: Common
side_effect_groups.summary: Dry mouth, nausea, bowel changes and trouble sleeping were the most common events in trials. Online sources add headache, dizziness and mood effects.

items.text: In a 24-week phase 2 trial in 203 obese adults, the most common adverse events with tesofensine were dry mouth, nausea, constipation, hard stools, diarrhea and insomnia.
items.label: research

items.text: In a small randomized trial of Tesomet in hypothalamic obesity, related events were mostly mild: sleep disturbances (50% vs 13% placebo), dry mouth (43% vs 0%) and headache (36% vs 0%), with one serious event of worsened anxiety.
items.label: research

items.text: A Wikipedia summary lists dry mouth, headache, nausea, insomnia, diarrhea and constipation as common adverse events with tesofensine, and notes small blood pressure and heart rate increases.
items.label: internet

items.text: Wikipedia says the withdrawal rate due to adverse events was 13% with tesofensine versus 6% with placebo.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with affiliate links to sellers, says common effects include dizziness, abdominal pain and anxiety, irritability or mood changes, and that about 71% of the 0.5 mg group completed 24 weeks with roughly 20% leaving over adverse events. These figures were not checked against the trial.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Heart rate and blood pressure
side_effect_groups.summary: Heart rate rose by several beats per minute in trials. Blood pressure changes were small at 0.5 mg or lower.

items.text: After 24 weeks, 0.25 mg and 0.5 mg showed no significant blood pressure increase versus placebo, while heart rate rose by 7.4 beats per minute at 0.5 mg.
items.label: research

items.text: In four 14-week trials, heart rate rose 2.1, 4.2, 6.0 and 6.8 beats per minute at 0.125 to 1.0 mg versus placebo, with no blood pressure effect.
items.label: research

items.text: Wikipedia says blood pressure increased modestly (1 to 3 mmHg) and heart rate by up to about 8 beats per minute.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Trial reporting concerns
side_effect_groups.summary: The journal that published the main obesity trial later issued an expression of concern, and the authors replied in a comment on under-reporting of adverse effects.

items.text: The Lancet published an expression of concern in 2013 for the 2008 phase 2 trial. The authors then published a comment titled 'Under-reporting of adverse effects of tesofensine'. The details were not available to review here.
items.label: research

side_effect_groups.title: Abuse potential
side_effect_groups.summary: A single-dose study in recreational stimulant users found abuse potential no greater than bupropion or atomoxetine.

items.text: In 52 recreational stimulant users, single-dose tesofensine did not differ significantly from placebo on abuse-related measures.
items.label: research

side_effect_groups.title: Regulatory status
side_effect_groups.summary: Not approved for sale anywhere, according to Wikipedia.

items.text: Wikipedia says tesofensine has not been approved for sale anywhere and, as of 2019, was an Investigational New Drug in the US.
items.label: internet
